newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds fall on profit-taking after rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds fall on profit-taking after rate hike.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks and bonds rose briefly Tuesday after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in two years, but the market turned lower as investors took profits after the widely expected move.
The dollar kept most of its earlier gains as higher rates make yields on U.S. investments more attractive.

"It's as expected. I think this means we ought to see a relief rally in both bonds and stocks over the course of the next few days," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.

Shortly after the Fed announced the rate hike at 2:14 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was off 5.66 points at 6,899.59. The blue-chip index rallied briefly after the report to gain nearly 30 points, but quickly slid 26.44 to 6,878.81 shortly before 3 p.m. EST.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines by a 13-11 margin on active New York Stock Exchange volume of 376 million shares.
The Nasdaq composite index was up 1.70 points at 1,244.34.
The Fed raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points at its policy-making meeting, in an effort to stay a step ahead of inflation and keep the economic expansion on track.

The increase brought the federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans up to 5.50 percent. The Fed left the discount rate it charges banks for money unchanged at 5.0 percent.

"This action was taken in light of persisting strength in demand, which is progressively increasing the risk of inflationary imbalances developing in the economy that would eventually undermine the long expansion," the Fed said in a statement.
The rate hike, the first since February 1995, is likely to lead to higher borrowing costs for many consumers and companies, from credit card users to the stores they shop at.

While higher interest rates tend to slow economic growth, Wall Street cheered the Fed's move because it seemed to be aimed at prolonging the economic expansion by stifling inflation before it became a problem.
"They're not trying to slow the economy down. They're trying to be sure that the economy doesn't produce inflationary pressures," said William Griggs, managing director, Griggs & Santow Inc.

In the bond market, the key 30-year Treasury bond jumped half a point before turning down 8/32, sending its yield up to 6.95 percent from Monday's close of 6.92 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The dollar rose to 1.6918 German marks and 123.60 Japanese yen from 1.6880 marks and 122.85 yen late Monday.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 blue chip share index finished 55.9 points higher at 4,270.7, just below the day's best levels. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average finished 395.79 points, or 2.19 percent, higher at 18,439.61.
